stem: The first major international conference on the human environment, which led to the creation of UNEP, was held in 1972 at:
solution: The 1972 United Nations Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm was the first global environment summit; it led to the founding of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) and is commemorated by World Environment Day (5 June).

stem: The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) is headquartered in:
solution: UNEP, the leading global environmental authority within the UN, is headquartered in Nairobi, Kenya — the first UN agency to be based in a developing country.

stem: World Environment Day is observed every year on:
solution: World Environment Day (5 June), led by UNEP, marks the anniversary of the 1972 Stockholm Conference and is the UN's flagship day for environmental awareness.

stem: The 1992 'Earth Summit' (UN Conference on Environment and Development) in Rio de Janeiro produced all of the following EXCEPT:
solution: The Rio Earth Summit (1992) opened the UNFCCC and CBD for signature and adopted Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration. The Montreal Protocol predates it (1987) and deals with ozone.

stem: 'Agenda 21', adopted at the Rio Earth Summit, is:
options: A non-binding global action plan for sustainable development in the 21st century
solution: Agenda 21 is a comprehensive, non-binding action plan for sustainable development to be implemented globally, nationally and locally by governments and organisations.

stem: The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) has three main objectives: conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components, and:
options: Fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from genetic resources
solution: The CBD's three goals are conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use, and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from the use of genetic resources (access and benefit-sharing).

stem: The Cartagena Protocol (2000) under the CBD deals with the safe handling and transboundary movement of:
solution: The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety governs the safe transfer, handling and use of Living Modified Organisms (products of modern biotechnology) that may affect biodiversity, using the precautionary approach.

stem: The Nagoya Protocol (2010) under the CBD addresses:
options: Access to genetic resources and fair, equitable sharing of benefits (ABS)
solution: The Nagoya Protocol provides a legal framework for Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS) — ensuring that benefits from using genetic resources are shared fairly with the countries and communities providing them.

stem: The 'Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework' (2022) set a headline target to protect what fraction of land and seas by 2030?
solution: The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted at CBD COP15, includes the '30x30' goal — conserving at least 30% of land, inland waters and coastal/marine areas by 2030.

stem: CITES, which regulates international trade in endangered species, stands for the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of:
solution: CITES (1973) — the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora — regulates cross-border trade to ensure it does not threaten species survival. Its secretariat is in Geneva.

stem: Under CITES, species threatened with extinction and barred from commercial international trade are listed in:
solution: CITES Appendix I lists species threatened with extinction; their commercial international trade is generally prohibited. Appendix II covers species that may become threatened; Appendix III covers species protected in at least one country.

stem: The Convention on Migratory Species (CMS), also called the Bonn Convention, protects:
options: Migratory species and their habitats across national boundaries
solution: The CMS (Bonn Convention, 1979) conserves migratory species (birds, marine mammals, etc.) that cross national borders, encouraging range states to cooperate. India hosted CMS COP13 in 2020 (Gandhinagar).

stem: India hosted the 13th Conference of Parties (COP13) of the CMS in 2020 at Gandhinagar; its mascot was the:
solution: CMS COP13 (Gandhinagar, 2020) had the Great Indian Bustard as its mascot 'Gibi', highlighting the plight of this critically endangered migratory bird.

stem: The Stockholm Convention (2001) targets the elimination or restriction of:
solution: The Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants restricts or eliminates POPs — toxic, long-lived, bioaccumulative chemicals (e.g. DDT, PCBs, dioxins) that travel globally.

stem: The Basel Convention (1989) regulates the transboundary movement of:
solution: The Basel Convention controls transboundary movements of hazardous and other wastes and their disposal, curbing the dumping of toxic waste from richer to poorer nations.

stem: The Rotterdam Convention promotes shared responsibility in the international trade of hazardous chemicals through the principle of:
solution: The Rotterdam Convention uses the Prior Informed Consent procedure, requiring exporters to obtain the importing country's informed agreement before shipping listed hazardous chemicals and pesticides.

stem: The 'Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm' conventions together form a cluster dealing broadly with:
options: Sound management of chemicals and hazardous wastes
solution: The BRS conventions (Basel–wastes, Rotterdam–chemical trade, Stockholm–POPs) are jointly administered to promote the environmentally sound management of chemicals and wastes throughout their life cycle.

stem: The Minamata Convention (2013) aims to protect human health and the environment from emissions of:
solution: The Minamata Convention on Mercury controls and reduces anthropogenic mercury emissions and releases, named after the Japanese city that suffered mercury poisoning. It restricts mercury mining, use and trade.

stem: The Vienna Convention (1985) is the framework treaty under which which protocol was adopted?
solution: The Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer (1985) is the framework under which the Montreal Protocol (1987) was adopted to phase out ozone-depleting substances.

stem: The UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) primarily addresses:
options: Land degradation and desertification, especially in drylands
solution: The UNCCD (1994), the third Rio Convention, combats desertification and land degradation and mitigates drought effects, particularly in Africa and other dryland regions. India hosted its COP14 in 2019.

stem: The three 'Rio Conventions' emerging from or linked to the 1992 Earth Summit are the UNFCCC, the CBD and the:
solution: The three Rio Conventions are the UNFCCC (climate), CBD (biodiversity) and UNCCD (desertification), reflecting the interlinked global environmental challenges identified at Rio.

stem: The IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature), which produces the Red List, is:
options: A union of governments and civil-society organisations focused on nature conservation
solution: The IUCN is a membership union of government and civil-society organisations, best known for the Red List of Threatened Species and for setting protected-area categories. Its headquarters is at Gland, Switzerland.

stem: The World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), known for its panda logo, is:
options: An international NGO working on wilderness preservation and reducing human impact on the environment
solution: WWF is a leading international non-governmental conservation organisation (panda logo), working on biodiversity, forests, oceans, wildlife and climate.

stem: The 'Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)', adopted in 2015, number:
solution: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development sets 17 SDGs (with 169 targets), succeeding the Millennium Development Goals. Several (e.g. SDG 13 Climate Action, 14 Life Below Water, 15 Life on Land) are environmental.

stem: The term 'Sustainable Development' was popularised by the 1987 report of the World Commission on Environment and Development, known as the:
solution: The Brundtland Report 'Our Common Future' (1987) defined sustainable development as development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

stem: The 'Global Environment Facility (GEF)' functions primarily as a:
options: Financial mechanism funding environmental projects in developing countries under several conventions
solution: The GEF provides funding to developing countries for projects addressing biodiversity, climate change, land degradation, chemicals and international waters, serving as a financial mechanism for the CBD, UNFCCC, UNCCD and others.

stem: The 'Green Climate Fund (GCF)' was established under the UNFCCC to:
options: Channel climate finance from developed to developing countries for mitigation and adaptation
solution: The Green Climate Fund helps developing countries reduce emissions and adapt to climate change, operationalising the goal of mobilising climate finance under the UNFCCC/Paris framework.

stem: The 'IPBES' is often called the 'IPCC for biodiversity'; it is the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and:
solution: IPBES (Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services) assesses the state of biodiversity and ecosystem services for policymakers, paralleling the IPCC's role for climate.

stem: The 'REDD+' mechanism under the UNFCCC incentivises developing countries to:
options: Reduce emissions from deforestation and forest degradation, and enhance forest carbon stocks
solution: REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation, plus conservation and sustainable forest management) provides results-based finance to developing countries that protect and enhance forest carbon sinks.

stem: The 'World Meteorological Organization (WMO)', a co-parent of the IPCC, is a specialised agency dealing with:
solution: The WMO is the UN specialised agency for weather, climate and the hydrological cycle; with UNEP it established the IPCC and coordinates global meteorological observation.

stem: India's flagship international grouping to make infrastructure resilient to disasters and climate is the:
solution: India launched the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) in 2019 to promote infrastructure systems that withstand climate and disaster risks; it is headquartered in New Delhi.

stem: The 'Ramsar', 'World Heritage' and 'Biosphere Reserve' designations are, respectively, associated with which bodies?
solution: Ramsar sites fall under the Ramsar Convention; World Heritage Sites under UNESCO's World Heritage Convention; and Biosphere Reserves under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme.

stem: The 'Bonn Challenge' is a global effort to:
options: Restore degraded and deforested land (forest landscape restoration)
solution: The Bonn Challenge aims to bring degraded and deforested landscapes into restoration (350 million hectares by 2030), contributing to climate, biodiversity and livelihood goals. India has made a large pledge under it.

stem: The 'One Sun One World One Grid (OSOWOG)' initiative, backed by India, envisions:
options: An interconnected transnational solar power grid
solution: OSOWOG proposes interconnecting solar energy grids across regions and countries so that 'the sun never sets' on the network, enabling reliable, round-the-clock renewable power sharing.

stem: The 'Paris Agreement' was concluded at which COP?
solution: The Paris Agreement was adopted at COP21 in Paris in December 2015. (COP3 gave the Kyoto Protocol; COP15 Copenhagen failed to reach a binding deal; COP26 was Glasgow 2021.)

stem: The 'Stern Review' (2006) is notable for framing climate change as:
options: The greatest and widest-ranging market failure, urging early economic action
solution: The Stern Review on the Economics of Climate Change argued that the costs of inaction far outweigh the costs of early action, describing climate change as the greatest market failure ever seen.

stem: Which organisation maintains the 'World Network of Biosphere Reserves'?
solution: UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme maintains the World Network of Biosphere Reserves. Twelve of India's biosphere reserves are part of this network.

stem: The 'Aichi Biodiversity Targets' were a set of 20 targets adopted under the CBD's Strategic Plan for:
solution: The Aichi Targets (adopted at Nagoya, 2010) formed the CBD's Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020. They were largely unmet, leading to the new Kunming-Montreal framework (2022).

stem: The 'High Seas Treaty' (BBNJ Agreement, 2023) aims to conserve biodiversity in:
options: Areas of the ocean beyond national jurisdiction (the high seas)
solution: The BBNJ (Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction) or 'High Seas Treaty' (2023) provides for conservation and sustainable use of marine biodiversity in international waters, including marine protected areas on the high seas.

stem: Which convention is directly responsible for the 'Montreux Record' of threatened wetlands?
solution: The Montreux Record is maintained under the Ramsar Convention, listing Ramsar sites whose ecological character is changing or likely to change due to human interference.

stem: The 'Kyoto Protocol' vs 'Paris Agreement' key difference is that Paris:
options: Is binding on developed countries only
Applies to all countries via nationally determined contributions (bottom-up), unlike Kyoto's top-down targets on developed nations
solution: Kyoto imposed top-down binding targets only on developed (Annex I) countries; Paris takes a universal, bottom-up approach where all countries submit their own NDCs, aiming for well below 2°C.

stem: The 'Doha Amendment' extended which climate treaty into a second commitment period?
solution: The Doha Amendment (2012) established the second commitment period of the Kyoto Protocol (2013–2020), though ratification was slow and its coverage limited.

stem: India's per-capita greenhouse-gas emissions, relevant to climate negotiations, are:
options: Well below the world average despite India's large total emissions
solution: India's per-capita emissions remain well below the global average and far below developed nations', a point India stresses in negotiations invoking equity and CBDR, even though its total emissions are among the highest due to population and development needs.

stem: 'Carbon markets' under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement allow countries to:
options: Cooperate and trade emission-reduction outcomes to meet their NDCs cost-effectively
solution: Article 6 provides mechanisms for voluntary cooperation, including trading Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs) and a centralised crediting mechanism, to help countries meet NDCs efficiently.

stem: The 'LeadIT' (Leadership Group for Industry Transition), co-founded by India and Sweden, focuses on decarbonising:
solution: LeadIT brings together countries and companies committed to low-carbon transition of hard-to-abate heavy industries such as steel and cement, targeting net-zero industrial emissions.

stem: Which UN body adopted the resolution recognising a 'clean, healthy and sustainable environment' as a human right in 2022?
solution: In 2022 the UN General Assembly adopted a landmark resolution recognising access to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment as a universal human right, building on an earlier Human Rights Council resolution.

stem: The 'Global Tiger Forum (GTF)', the only inter-governmental body for tiger conservation, is headquartered in:
solution: The Global Tiger Forum, the sole intergovernmental international body dedicated to tiger conservation among tiger-range countries, is headquartered in New Delhi, India.

stem: The 'CoP' host and the '30x30' target are associated with which convention's 2022 summit?
solution: The '30x30' target is the flagship of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework adopted at CBD COP15 (2022), presided over by China and held in Montreal.

stem: Which of the following correctly pairs a convention with its subject? (i) CITES – wildlife trade (ii) Ramsar – wetlands (iii) Basel – hazardous waste
solution: All three pairings are correct: CITES governs trade in endangered species, Ramsar protects wetlands, and Basel regulates transboundary hazardous-waste movement.
